notebooks.title: Limitations of Automated Epistemic Self-Correction
notebooks.summary: Analysis of automated decision-making and cognitive systems indicates that while algorithmic frameworks can process complex tasks, identifying and revising foundational methodological assumptions typically requires external oversight and normative evaluation.
notebooks.findings: Automated decision-making systems introduce significant ethical and operational challenges when delegating high-stakes tasks without external auditing. [source-43c0a60d013d4369]
notebooks.limitations: The available literature examines ethics-based auditing and cognitive offloading rather than direct empirical demonstrations of autonomous methodological self-correction.
notebooks.next_questions: What formal architectures would enable an automated system to reliably surface and test its own foundational premises?
notebooks.reason: Synthesizing available source material on automated decision-making and cognitive extension to address the project question.

review.alternative: Automated systems might achieve internal consistency without external audits if provided with explicit normative feedback loops.
review.would_change_mind: Empirical evidence of an automated system independently discovering and correcting a flawed foundational premise without human intervention.

claims.statement: Automated decision-making systems introduce significant ethical and operational challenges when delegating high-stakes tasks without external auditing.

support.explanation: Demonstrates that automated systems operate under delegated authority and face structural limitations requiring external ethical oversight.
support.passage: Important decisions that impact human lives, livelihoods, and the natural environment are increasingly being automated. Delegating tasks to so -called automated decision-making systems (ADMS) can improve efficiency and enable new solutions. However, these benefits are coupled with ethical challenges.

review.alternative: Automated systems might achieve internal consistency without external audits if provided with explicit normative feedback loops.
review.would_change_mind: Empirical evidence of an automated system independently discovering and correcting a flawed foundational premise without human intervention.

support_provenance.statement: Automated decision-making systems introduce significant ethical and operational challenges when delegating high-stakes tasks without external auditing.

notebooks.title: AI Dependence and Reduced Autonomy in Athletes
notebooks.summary: Recent cross-sectional evidence indicates that dependence on AI training recommendations is positively associated with body signal outsourcing, which correlates with reduced self-regulation, decision hesitation, and diminished training self-efficacy.
notebooks.findings:
AI training recommendation dependence is positively associated with body signal outsourcing tendency in athletes. [source-18d0eec713c84bb4]

Body signal outsourcing links to a reduced sense of self-regulation and increased training decision hesitation. [source-d9addfec171d4b5d]
notebooks.limitations: The findings are derived from cross-sectional questionnaire data, meaning causal directions remain provisional and require longitudinal tracking.
notebooks.next_questions: What are the longitudinal impacts of sustained AI training recommendation dependence on long-term athlete autonomy and self-regulation?
notebooks.reason: Revising notebook nb-emergent-prefs-001 using newly incorporated evidence from Chen (2026) to detail the serial association model.

review.alternative: Athletes who already outsource bodily signals may naturally seek out AI tools that match their existing preferences.
review.would_change_mind: Longitudinal experimental data showing that reduced AI reliance reverses body signal outsourcing.

claims.statement: AI training recommendation dependence is positively associated with body signal outsourcing tendency in athletes.

support.explanation: The source demonstrates a direct positive association between reliance on AI training recommendations and outsourcing internal bodily signals.
support.passage: AI training recommendation dependence was significantly and positively associated with body signal outsourcing tendency

review.alternative: Decision hesitation could stem from general competitive anxiety rather than AI tool dependence specifically.
review.would_change_mind: Controlled studies isolating AI feedback from general coaching feedback.

claims.statement: Body signal outsourcing links to a reduced sense of self-regulation and increased training decision hesitation.

support.explanation: The study's structural equation modeling links outsourcing to lower self-regulation and increased hesitation.
support.passage: body signal outsourcing tendency, which was, in turn, positively associated with a reduced sense of self-regulation. A reduced sense of self-regulation was positively associated with training decision hesitation

review.alternative: Athletes who already outsource bodily signals may naturally seek out AI tools that match their existing preferences.
review.would_change_mind: Longitudinal experimental data showing that reduced AI reliance reverses body signal outsourcing.

support_provenance.statement: AI training recommendation dependence is positively associated with body signal outsourcing tendency in athletes.

review.alternative: Decision hesitation could stem from general competitive anxiety rather than AI tool dependence specifically.
review.would_change_mind: Controlled studies isolating AI feedback from general coaching feedback.

support_provenance.statement: Body signal outsourcing links to a reduced sense of self-regulation and increased training decision hesitation.

research.reason: Current findings are based on cross-sectional data; longitudinal research is required to determine the causal trajectory of AI dependence on athlete autonomy.

detail.title: Limitations of Automated Epistemic Self-Correction
detail.summary: Analysis of automated decision-making and cognitive systems indicates that while algorithmic frameworks can process complex tasks, identifying and revising foundational methodological assumptions typically requires external oversight and normative evaluation.
detail.findings: Automated decision-making systems introduce significant ethical and operational challenges when delegating high-stakes tasks without external auditing. [source-43c0a60d013d4369]
detail.limitations: The available literature examines ethics-based auditing and cognitive offloading rather than direct empirical demonstrations of autonomous methodological self-correction.
detail.next_questions: What formal architectures would enable an automated system to reliably surface and test its own foundational premises?
detail.reason: Synthesizing available source material on automated decision-making and cognitive extension to address the project question.

review.alternative: Automated systems might achieve internal consistency without external audits if provided with explicit normative feedback loops.
review.would_change_mind: Empirical evidence of an automated system independently discovering and correcting a flawed foundational premise without human intervention.

detail.title: AI Dependence and Reduced Autonomy in Athletes
detail.summary: Recent cross-sectional evidence indicates that dependence on AI training recommendations is positively associated with body signal outsourcing, which correlates with reduced self-regulation, decision hesitation, and diminished training self-efficacy.
detail.findings:
AI training recommendation dependence is positively associated with body signal outsourcing tendency in athletes. [source-18d0eec713c84bb4]

Body signal outsourcing links to a reduced sense of self-regulation and increased training decision hesitation. [source-d9addfec171d4b5d]
detail.limitations: The findings are derived from cross-sectional questionnaire data, meaning causal directions remain provisional and require longitudinal tracking.
detail.next_questions: What are the longitudinal impacts of sustained AI training recommendation dependence on long-term athlete autonomy and self-regulation?
